title: The Roman–Parthian World
subtitle: 63 BC–224 AD · Rome and the Arsacids on the Euphrates: Carrhae, the Buffer Kingdoms, the Caravan Cities and the Fall of the Parthian House

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Pompey and the eastern settlement, the Roman emperors and the Arsacid kings, and the client kings of Armenia, Judaea, Commagene, Osroene and Palmyra

entries.label: Pompey's settlement of the East
entries.hint: Pompey, after defeating Mithridates VI and Tigranes of Armenia, abolished the Seleucid kingdom, made Syria a Roman province in 64 BC, took Jerusalem in 63 and organised a ring of client kingdoms (Armenia, Commagene, Osroene, Judaea) between the province and the Parthian empire; the Euphrates became the frontier of Rome with the Arsacids, in a system that lasted for a century.
entries.note: Appian, Mithridatic Wars 114–117; Plutarch, Pompey 38–45; Fergus Millar, The Roman Near East 31 BC–AD 337 (1993); Erich Gruen in The Cambridge Ancient History vol. 9 (1994).

entries.label: Augustus and the settlement of 20 BC
entries.hint: Augustus, who had refused to go to war to avenge Crassus, went to the East in 22–19 BC, and in 20 BC Tiberius received from Phraates IV the legionary standards lost at Carrhae and later prisoners, which Augustus treated as a great victory and commemorated on coins, the Prima Porta statue and the temple of Mars the Avenger; Armenia was given a client king and Roman protection.
entries.note: Res Gestae 29; Cassius Dio 54.8; Ovid, Fasti 5.579–598; Millar 1993.

entries.label: Trajan
entries.hint: Trajan, who had added Dacia and Arabia Petraea to the empire, left Rome in 113 on a campaign to depose the Parthian-supported king of Armenia, annexed Armenia in 114 and Mesopotamia in 115 and took Ctesiphon in 116, sailing down to the Persian Gulf; the provinces rose in revolt behind him and he abandoned most of the conquests in 117, dying on the way home in Cilicia.
entries.note: Cassius Dio 68.17–33; Eutropius 8.3; Fergus Millar 1993; Anthony Birley, Hadrian (1997).

entries.label: Septimius Severus and Caracalla
entries.hint: Septimius Severus, after defeating his rivals, campaigned against Vologases V in 195 and 197–199, took Seleucia and Ctesiphon in 198 and made northern Mesopotamia a province with the garrison city of Nisibis; his son Caracalla, who claimed in 216 the daughter of the Parthian king, invaded Parthia, was murdered near Carrhae in April 217 and was succeeded by Macrinus, who made a peace with Artabanus IV.
entries.note: Cassius Dio 75–79; Herodian 3–4; Millar 1993; Maurice Sartre, The Middle East under Rome (2005).

entries.label: Orodes II and Phraates IV
entries.hint: Orodes II (57–38 BC), who had the general Surenas defeat Crassus at Carrhae, and Phraates IV (38–2 BC), who survived the Roman attack of Antony and sent his sons to Augustus as pledges, ruled Parthia from Ctesiphon, which had replaced Seleucia as the winter capital, over a loose confederacy of satrapies and vassal kingdoms held together by the Arsacid house and the great families of Suren, Karen and Mihran.
entries.note: Plutarch, Crassus; Josephus, Antiquities 18; Marek Olbrycht, Parthia and the Arsacids (2021); Edward Dąbrowa, The Arsacids and Their State (2012).

entries.label: Vologases I
entries.hint: Vologases I, who came to the throne after a series of dynastic quarrels and the rival Vardanes, put his brother Tiridates on the throne of Armenia in 54, fought the Romans under Corbulo in 54–63, established a Parthian prince in Armenia under a Roman crown at Rhandeia and founded the town of Vologesias near Ctesiphon, minting coins with Aramaic and the first Pahlavi legends; his reign saw a revival of Persian tradition and the collection of the Avesta.
entries.note: Tacitus, Annals 12–15; Josephus, Jewish War; Cassius Dio 63; Olbrycht 2021.

entries.label: Osroene and Edessa
entries.hint: The kingdom of Osroene, ruled from Edessa (Urfa) by the Arab Abgarid house from 132 BC, was a client of Parthia and Rome in turn, with a population speaking Syriac, and its king Abgar V was said in a later tradition to have corresponded with Jesus; Caracalla annexed it in 213 and the state became a Roman colony and then a province under Gordian III in 244.
entries.note: Eusebius, Church History 1.13; Han J. W. Drijvers, Cults and Beliefs at Edessa (1980); Steven Ross, Roman Edessa (2001).

entries.label: Hatra, Adiabene, Characene and Commagene
entries.hint: The small kingdoms on the borders held positions between the great powers: Commagene, with its hilltop sanctuary of Nemrut Dagh, was annexed in AD 72; Adiabene, whose royal house converted to Judaism, was a Parthian vassal; Characene at the head of the Gulf, with its capital Spasinou Charax, held the sea trade; and Hatra, the walled city of the Arab kings of the desert, which twice repelled Roman sieges in AD 117 and 198–199, fell to the Sasanians about 240.
entries.note: Josephus, Antiquities 20; Cassius Dio 68, 75; Hatra inscriptions; Millar 1993; Lucinda Dirven (ed.), Hatra (2013).

entries.label: The kings of Armenia
entries.hint: Armenia, a kingdom between the empires, was taken by Rome in the reign of Tigranes the Great, held by Roman nominees under Augustus and Tiberius and fell to the Parthian prince Tiridates in 54; after the compromise at Rhandeia in 63 he received his crown from Nero in Rome in 66, and from then until 224 the country was ruled by the Arsacid branch, under a nominal Roman suzerainty, an arrangement that survived until Trajan and was re-established by Hadrian.
entries.note: Tacitus, Annals 13–15; Cassius Dio 62–63; Nina Garsoïan, in The Armenian People vol. 1 (1997); Robert Hewsen, Armenia: A Historical Atlas (2001).

entries.label: Herod and the Judaean kingdom
entries.hint: Herod, named king of Judaea by the Senate in 40 BC, took Jerusalem in 37 with Roman troops, and ruled until 4 BC as a client of Antony and then Augustus, building Caesarea, Sebaste, Masada, Herodium and the new Temple; after the Roman province of Judaea (AD 6–66) and the kingdom of Agrippa I and II, the Jewish revolt of 66 ended the arrangement.
entries.note: Josephus, Jewish War 1, Antiquities 14–17; Peter Richardson, Herod the Great (1996); Millar 1993.

entries.label: Palmyra
entries.hint: Palmyra, an oasis on the road from the Euphrates to Damascus, was brought within Rome's sphere when Germanicus' legate Creticus Silanus put it under Rome's supervision about AD 17, received the title of a free city under Hadrian in 129 and a colony under the Severans; a council of citizens and its tribal elders ran the city, and its merchants and their caravans controlled the trade between the Euphrates and the Mediterranean.
entries.note: Palmyrene Tariff (AD 137; Matthews, 1984); Pliny, Natural History 5.88; Andreas Schmidt-Colinet; Millar 1993.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Carrhae, the Parthian invasion of 40 BC, Antony's retreat, the war over Armenia, Trajan's conquests, the Parthian war of Verus and Severus' Ctesiphon

entries.label: Carrhae
entries.hint: Crassus, who had crossed the Euphrates in 54 to win a reputation in the East, led some 40,000 men into the Mesopotamian steppe, and on 9 June 53 BC the Parthian general Surenas surrounded his legionaries with 1,000 cataphracts and 9,000 horse archers whose arrows, supplied by a baggage train of camels, exhausted them; Crassus was killed in the parley, 20,000 Romans died and 10,000 were captured and settled in Margiana.
entries.note: Plutarch, Crassus 17–33; Cassius Dio 40.16–27; Lionel Wilcox; Gareth Sampson, The Defeat of Rome (2008).

entries.label: The Parthian invasion of Syria and Antony's Median campaign
entries.hint: Pacorus, son of Orodes II, and the Roman exile Quintus Labienus invaded Syria and Judaea in 40 BC and held them for two years until Ventidius Bassus defeated them in 38; in 36 Antony led 100,000 men across Armenia into Media Atropatene, lost his baggage train and siege engines and, after a retreat in winter in which he lost a quarter of his army, pulled out.
entries.note: Plutarch, Antony 33–51; Cassius Dio 48–49; Sampson 2008; Olbrycht 2021.

entries.label: The Armenian war of Corbulo
entries.hint: When Vologases I put his brother Tiridates on the Armenian throne in 54, Nero's general Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo took Artaxata in 58 and Tigranocerta in 59, put a Roman candidate on the throne, and after Paetus's defeat at Rhandeia in 62 won a compromise by which Tiridates should receive his crown from Nero; he came to Rome in 66 with a retinue of 3,000 and was crowned by Nero in a great public ceremony.
entries.note: Tacitus, Annals 13–15; Cassius Dio 62–63; Millar 1993.

entries.label: The Jewish revolt and Vespasian's eastern settlement
entries.hint: The Jewish uprising against the procurator Gessius Florus in 66 spread to the whole of Judaea and brought Vespasian and Titus with some 60,000 men; Jerusalem was taken and the Temple burned in August 70 and Masada fell in 73 or 74, and the province was held by a legion, with tens of thousands killed and enslaved; the Parthian king Vologases offered help to Vespasian, and the Jews of Babylonia hoped for relief.
entries.note: Josephus, Jewish War; Martin Goodman, The Ruling Class of Judaea (1987); Millar 1993.

entries.label: Trajan's Parthian war
entries.hint: In reply to the Parthian king Osroes' installation of an Arsacid king in Armenia, Trajan took Armenia in 114, Mesopotamia in 115, Seleucia and Ctesiphon in 116, with the golden throne and the king's daughter, and went down the Tigris to the Gulf, where he saw a ship leaving for India and is reported to have wished to be young as Alexander; revolts in Mesopotamia, Judaea, Cyrenaica and Egypt, and the defeat at Hatra, broke the conquest, and Hadrian gave up the new provinces.
entries.note: Cassius Dio 68.17–33; Fronto; Eutropius; Birley 1997; Millar 1993.

entries.label: The Jewish revolts of the Diaspora and Bar Kokhba
entries.hint: The Jewish revolts in Cyrenaica, Egypt, Cyprus and Mesopotamia in 115–117 were put down by Quietus and Marcius Turbo with great loss of life; in 132–135 Simon bar Kokhba led a revolt in Judaea against Hadrian's plans for Aelia Capitolina, which cost, according to Cassius Dio, 580,000 dead and the depopulation of the province, and led to its renaming as Syria Palaestina.
entries.note: Cassius Dio 68.32, 69.12–14; Eusebius, Church History 4.2; Peter Schäfer, The Bar Kokhba War Reconsidered (2003); Hanan Eshel.

entries.label: The Parthian war of Lucius Verus
entries.hint: Vologases IV invaded Armenia and defeated a legion at Elegeia in 161, and Marcus Aurelius sent his co-emperor Lucius Verus, whose generals Statius Priscus, Avidius Cassius and Martius Verus took Artaxata in 163, Seleucia and Ctesiphon in 165 and burned the Parthian palace; the army carried the plague home, and Mesopotamia west of the Khabur became Roman.
entries.note: Historia Augusta, Verus; Cassius Dio 71–72; Lucian, How to Write History; Anthony Birley, Marcus Aurelius (1966).

entries.label: Severus's war and the sack of Ctesiphon
entries.hint: Severus, seizing the chance of the Parthian king Vologases V's support for Pescennius Niger, marched in 195 into Mesopotamia and in 197–198 took Ctesiphon, carried off a great booty and captives and put Roman garrisons at Nisibis and Singara; his failure to take Hatra in 198 and 199 despite two sieges is the famous exception.
entries.note: Cassius Dio 75.1–3, 76.9–12; Herodian 3.9, 3.1–3; Millar 1993.

entries.label: Macrinus and Nisibis
entries.hint: After the death of Caracalla in April 217, the Parthian king Artabanus IV advanced against the new emperor Macrinus, defeated him in three days of fighting at Nisibis in July 217, and in the peace that followed received a payment of 200 million sesterces, a defeat which weakened both states and helped Ardashir's revolt in Persis.
entries.note: Cassius Dio 79.26–27; Herodian 4.15; Olbrycht 2021.

entries.label: Ardashir's victory at Hormizdagan
entries.hint: Ardashir, son of Papak, a local ruler in Fars who had taken over Persis from the Arsacid vassals, defeated and killed the Parthian king Artabanus IV in a battle at Hormizdagan on the Susiana plain, according to later Sasanian tradition, and in 226 was crowned at Ctesiphon as King of Kings; the Arsacid line was replaced by the Sasanians, a dynasty with a very different notion of the imperial and religious order.
entries.note: Tabari, History; Res Gestae Divi Saporis; Josef Wiesehöfer, Ancient Persia (1996); Touraj Daryaee, Sasanian Persia (2009).

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The provincial settlement, the Euphrates frontier, the satrapal order of the Arsacids and the diplomacy of hostages and standards

entries.label: The provincial order of Roman Syria and Arabia
entries.hint: Roman Syria was made a province in 64 BC with a legate and legions at Antioch and in the north; Judaea after AD 6 with a prefect, Arabia Petraea after the annexation of Nabataea in 106, with its capital at Bostra and a new road, the Via Nova Traiana, from Bostra to Aila; the cities of the Decapolis, Antioch, Damascus and Apamea kept their civic institutions.
entries.note: Millar 1993; Glen Bowersock, Roman Arabia (1983); Sartre 2005.

entries.label: The Euphrates frontier
entries.hint: The Roman line along the Euphrates, with legions at Samosata, Zeugma, Melitene, Satala and later Raphaneae and Sura and the forts of the Syrian desert, supported client kingdoms and the system of paid allies, among them the Ituraeans and Emesa; the border was marked by trade tariffs, taxes at Zeugma and the use of the river as a boundary and a route.
entries.note: Millar 1993; Benjamin Isaac, The Limits of Empire (1990); David Kennedy, The Roman Army in Jordan (2004).

entries.label: The Arsacid monarchy and the satrapies
entries.hint: The Parthian empire, which the Greek sources call the kingdom of the Arsaces, had a king of kings, a council of the royal family and nobles and the clergy (the Megistanes), and a hierarchy of vassal kings, satraps and cities with their own rule, which paid tribute and military service; its weakness in the second century was the independence of the great houses and the succession disputes, which Rome exploited.
entries.note: Isidore of Charax, Parthian Stations; Josephus, Antiquities 18; Dąbrowa 2012; Olbrycht 2021.

entries.label: Hostages and standards
entries.hint: The rule between Rome and Parthia that the princes of the Arsacid house were sent to be educated and held in Rome as pledges, the four sons of Phraates IV in 10–9 BC, and the symbolic return of the Roman standards in 20 BC, created a system of ritualised relations in which each court claimed to be the superior; the Romans' choice of a king in Parthia from among the hostages was often a means of intervention.
entries.note: Strabo 16.1.28; Josephus, Antiquities 18; Tacitus, Annals 2; Millar 1993.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Zoroastrian and Greek cults, the Jewish revolts and diaspora, Mithras and the early churches of Edessa

entries.label: The Zoroastrian and Greek cults of the Arsacids
entries.hint: The Arsacid kings were tolerant patrons of many cults, with Greek gods and royal ancestor cults, as in the Nisa ostraca and the royal tombs, and Zoroastrian priests, magi and sacred fires; the god Hercules/Verethragna and Mithra, Bel and Nanaya, Shamash and the Arab gods of Hatra, among them Allat and the sun god, were worshipped, and the later Sasanian tradition said that Vologases ordered the first collection of the Avesta.
entries.note: Nisa ostraca; Hatra inscriptions; Mary Boyce, A History of Zoroastrianism vol. 3 (1991); Dirven 2013.

entries.label: The Jews of Babylonia
entries.hint: The Jewish communities of Babylonia, which had been there since the exile of 586 BC, grew in numbers and importance after the destruction of Jerusalem under the tolerant Parthian kings, with their exilarch and academies at Nehardea and Nisibis, and in the early third century, with Rav and Samuel, became the centre of the oral law that was written in the Babylonian Talmud; the royal house of Adiabene had joined the Jewish people in the first century.
entries.note: Josephus, Antiquities 20; Jacob Neusner, A History of the Jews in Babylonia vol. 1 (1965); Geoffrey Herman, A Prince without a Kingdom (2012).

entries.label: Mithras and the soldiers' cults
entries.hint: The cult of Mithras, a Roman mystery religion, drew on the Iranian god Mithra and spread among the army, with many Mithraea in the Danubian and Rhine provinces and a Mithraeum at Dura-Europos built in AD 168 and enlarged in 209; at Dura the garrison also worshipped the gods of Palmyra, Rome and the emperor.
entries.note: Franz Cumont, Textes et monuments figurés relatifs aux mystères de Mithra (1896); Michael Rostovtzeff, Dura-Europos and Its Art (1938); Clark Hopkins, The Discovery of Dura-Europos (1979).

entries.label: The early churches of Edessa and Dura-Europos
entries.hint: The Christian community of Edessa, with its Syriac scriptures and the writer Bardaisan (154–222), who debated fate and freedom in a Parthian court, was one of the first Christian communities east of the Euphrates; the house church of Dura-Europos, converted from a private house about 240–256 with a baptistery and wall paintings of the Good Shepherd and Healing the Paralytic, is the oldest identified church building.
entries.note: Book of the Laws of the Countries (Bardaisan); Carl Kraeling, The Excavations at Dura-Europos: The Christian Building (1967); Drijvers 1980.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The Parthian palaces and statues, Palmyrene tombs, Hatra and the Dura-Europos paintings

entries.label: The palace of Nisa and the Parthian art
entries.hint: The Parthian royal residence at Old Nisa near Ashgabat, with its Square House, the Round Hall and the ivory drinking horns (rhyta) carved with Greek scenes, and the great hall of Ctesiphon with its iwan, which in the Parthian period took the shape that dominated later Iranian architecture, show a court art that combined Hellenistic forms with Iranian taste; the frontal pose of figures in Parthian art is a feature in the wall paintings.
entries.note: Nisa excavations (Pugachenkova; Invernizzi); Vesta Curtis and Sarah Stewart (eds.), The Age of the Parthians (2007).

entries.label: Palmyrene tombs and sculpture
entries.hint: The temple of Bel, dedicated in AD 32, the colonnaded street with its tetrapylon, the temples of Baalshamin and Allat, the tower tombs and underground hypogea with portraits of the dead in limestone in a frontal Parthian style, and their bilingual inscriptions in Greek and Palmyrene Aramaic, show the Roman and Parthian elements of the culture; the tomb of the Three Brothers is one of the best preserved.
entries.note: Palmyrene inscriptions (Inventaire); Rubina Raja, Urban Development and Regional Identity (2012); Michael Seyrig.

entries.label: The paintings of Dura-Europos
entries.hint: The garrison town on the Euphrates, taken by the Parthians in about 113 BC and the Romans in AD 165 and destroyed by Shapur I in 256, has painted temples of the Palmyrene gods, the Mithraeum, the Christian house church and the synagogue of AD 244–245 with some 60 panels of biblical scenes, the earliest known figural cycle of Jewish art, which were found under the earth of the siege ramp in 1932.
entries.note: Dura-Europos excavation reports (Yale/French Academy, 1928–1937); Rostovtzeff 1938; Hopkins 1979; Susan Matheson, Dura-Europos (1982).

entries.label: The temples of Hatra
entries.hint: Hatra, a round walled city in the Jazira desert some 320 hectares, with the great iwans of the temple of Shamash, a sacred precinct of some 30 temples, the statues of kings and nobles with Parthian dress and its Aramaic inscriptions, held out against Trajan in 117 and Severus in 198–199 with its priest-kings, the Sanatruq and the Abdsimya, until its fall about 240.
entries.note: Hatra inscriptions (Aggoula, 1991); Dirven 2013; Cassius Dio 75.11–12.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Strabo's geography, Josephus, Palmyrene and Syriac literature and the Greek of the Arsacid court

entries.label: Strabo's Geography and the Parthian Stations
entries.hint: Strabo of Amasia described in his Geography of about 20 BC–AD 20 the Parthian lands and their position on the world's roads, and Isidore of Charax, in the Parthian Stations of the first century AD, listed the staging posts on the road from Zeugma on the Euphrates to Alexandria in Arachosia, the main Greek source on Parthian geography.
entries.note: Strabo, Geography 11, 16; Isidore of Charax, Parthian Stations (ed. Schoff, 1914).

entries.label: Syriac and Palmyrene Aramaic
entries.hint: Aramaic dialects in several scripts became the language of administration and cult in the border lands: Palmyrene, Hatran and Edessene Syriac, with Greek as a prestige language; the earliest dated Syriac inscription is from Birecik (AD 6), and the Syriac literature of Bardaisan's school, with the first Christian hymns and translations of the Gospels, followed in the second and third centuries.
entries.note: Syriac inscriptions (Drijvers and Healey, 1999); Sebastian Brock, The Hidden Pearl (2001).

entries.label: Roman writers on the Parthians
entries.hint: Roman and Greek authors from Horace and Virgil to Tacitus, Cassius Dio and Herodian represented the Parthians as a threat of horse archers and decadent tyrants but also respected their statecraft, and the memory of Carrhae haunted Roman poetry for a century; the question whether Parthia was a great power or a nuisance is argued by modern historians.
entries.note: Horace, Odes 3.5; Virgil, Georgics 3; Tacitus, Annals; Cassius Dio; Sampson 2008.

entries.label: Josephus
entries.hint: Flavius Josephus, a Jewish priest who commanded in Galilee in 66, was captured by Vespasian, prophesied his rise to the throne, and later in Rome wrote the Jewish War (c. 75–79), the Antiquities (93–94) and Against Apion, an account in Greek of the revolt, of the Herodian kings and of the Jewish diaspora, including the Parthian world, that is the main source for the period.
entries.note: Josephus, Jewish War; Antiquities; Life; Tessa Rajak, Josephus: The Historian and His Society (1983).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The silk and spice routes, the tolls of Charax and Palmyra and the Roman garrison economy

entries.label: The silk road through Parthia
entries.hint: Silk from Han China crossed Central Asia to Parthia, whose merchants and tolls controlled the overland road from Merv to the Euphrates, as Pliny complains that Rome lost a hundred million sesterces a year to India, China and Arabia; the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea about AD 50 describes the competing sea route, and Isidore's stations list the posts of the land road.
entries.note: Pliny, Natural History 6.101, 12.84; Periplus Maris Erythraei; Valerie Hansen, The Silk Road (2012).

entries.label: The tolls of Palmyra and Charax
entries.hint: The Tariff of Palmyra, a long inscription in Greek and Palmyrene of AD 137, set the duties on imports, slaves, purple, oil, perfume and dried fish in the city, and the Palmyrene merchants had colonies in Seleucia, Vologesias, Charax, Dura, Coptos, Rome and Gaul; Charax, the port at the mouth of the Tigris and Euphrates, was the base of the trade with India.
entries.note: Palmyrene Tariff (Matthews, Journal of Roman Studies 74, 1984); Gary Young, Rome's Eastern Trade (2001); Raschke 1978.

entries.label: The Roman army in the East and its economy
entries.hint: The garrisons of the East, with four legions in Syria and later two in Mesopotamia, and their numbers of auxiliaries, which in total were some 60,000 men, were a main part of the local economy, with their pay, requisitions, the purchase of grain and the veterans' settlement; the papyri of Dura and Roman Egypt show the rations and supply of units and contracts with local merchants.
entries.note: Dura papyri (Pap. Dura 100, 101); Millar 1993; Isaac 1990.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The cataphract and the Parthian shot, siege engineering at Dura and the limes

entries.label: The cataphract and the Parthian shot
entries.hint: The Parthian army combined heavy cavalry (cataphracts) armed with long lances and with scale armour for horse and rider and the light horse archers who could shoot backwards while feigning retreat, the Parthian shot; the composite bow and the use of camels to supply arrows meant that infantry armies lacking cavalry could be exhausted on the steppe.
entries.note: Plutarch, Crassus 24–27; Justin 41; Dura-Europos graffiti of a cataphract; Karen Dixon and Pat Southern, The Late Roman Army (1996).

entries.label: The siege of Dura-Europos and the mines
entries.hint: The archaeological evidence from the last siege of Dura by the Sasanians in 256 shows the oldest known use of siege mining and countermining in the Near East, with the bodies of Roman soldiers killed in the tunnels, and a massive earth ramp built against the walls; the Persian army used siege towers and tunnelling, and the finds of armour and horse barding are among the best of the age.
entries.note: Simon James, The Excavations at Dura-Europos: The Arms and Armour (2004); Rostovtzeff; Hopkins 1979.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The return of the standards, the embassies to Han China and Rome, the hostages and the caravan treaties

entries.label: The Parthian hostages and Roman princes
entries.hint: Phraates IV sent four sons, with their wives and children, to Augustus in 10–9 BC as pledges, and later, when the Parthians sought a king from Rome, Vonones I was sent back in AD 8 and ruled four years; the exiled Parthian princes in Rome were an instrument in the political game of the two courts.
entries.note: Josephus, Antiquities 18.39–52; Strabo 16.1.28; Res Gestae 32; Millar 1993.

entries.label: The embassy of Gan Ying and the Han
entries.hint: The Chinese general Ban Chao sent his envoy Gan Ying in AD 97 from the Tarim basin to the Roman Orient (Da Qin), who got as far as the shore of the Persian Gulf, where the Parthian sailors told him the voyage would take two years and he turned back; the Chinese histories of the Later Han record Parthia as Anxi and the Roman empire as Da Qin.
entries.note: Hou Hanshu 88; Hansen 2012; Michael Loewe.

entries.label: The Kushans and the Roman embassies to India and China
entries.hint: Kushan emperors, Kanishka and his successors, held the lands between Parthia and India and mediated the traffic of the Silk Road and the Indian Ocean; Roman embassies to China are reported by the Hou Hanshu in AD 166, which claims that merchants in the name of the emperor Andun (Marcus Aurelius Antoninus) came from the south by sea and brought ivory, rhinoceros horn and tortoise shell.
entries.note: Hou Hanshu 88; Periplus; Hansen 2012.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The Antonine plague, the earthquake of Antioch and the shifting Euphrates

entries.label: The earthquake of Antioch
entries.hint: While Trajan was staying at Antioch on the eve of his Parthian campaign, a violent earthquake on 13 December 115 destroyed much of the city, killed many including the consul Pedo and injured the emperor, who escaped through a window; the damage and the repairs, which Hadrian continued, are in Cassius Dio and Malalas, and the Antioch region lies on the Dead Sea Transform fault.
entries.note: Cassius Dio 68.24–25; Malalas 11; Nicholas Ambraseys, Earthquakes in the Mediterranean and Middle East (2009).

entries.label: The Antonine plague
entries.hint: A plague that came with the army from Seleucia in 165 after Verus's Parthian war and spread throughout the Roman empire, which Galen described, killed perhaps 5 to 10 per cent of the population of the empire at its height and, according to Cassius Dio, 2,000 a day in Rome in AD 189; it probably was smallpox, and the Parthian side also suffered.
entries.note: Galen, Methodus medendi; Cassius Dio 72.14, 73.14; Historia Augusta, Verus 8; Kyle Harper, The Fate of Rome (2017).

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Queen Musa, Queen Helena of Adiabene, the garrison soldiers, the caravaneers and the exiles

entries.label: The Roman captives of Carrhae and Margiana
entries.hint: The 10,000 Roman prisoners of Carrhae were settled, according to Pliny and Plutarch, in Margiana (Merv) as frontier troops against the nomads, where they married local women and passed from sight; one hypothesis of the 1950s, now generally rejected, put some of them as founders of a Chinese town of Liqian in Gansu, but the evidence for the identification is poor.
entries.note: Pliny, Natural History 6.46; Plutarch, Crassus 31; Horace, Odes 3.5; Sampson 2008.

entries.label: Queen Musa of Parthia
entries.hint: Musa, an Italian slave girl sent to Phraates IV as a gift by Augustus about 20 BC, became his queen, bore Phraataces, and with her son poisoned the king and ruled with him as consort and co-ruler in 2 BC; coins of the pair, with her portrait and the legend Thea Musa Ourania, have survived, and in AD 4 both were deposed by a revolt of the nobles for the offence of an incestuous marriage.
entries.note: Josephus, Antiquities 18.40–43; Coins of Phraataces and Musa; Olbrycht 2021.

entries.label: Helena of Adiabene
entries.hint: Queen Helena of Adiabene, wife and sister of King Monobazus, adopted the Jewish religion about AD 30 with her son Izates and the court, went to Jerusalem in a famine in 46–47 and bought grain from Egypt and figs from Cyprus for the poor, built a palace in the city and was buried in the tombs of the queen's mausoleum, the so-called Tomb of the Kings.
entries.note: Josephus, Antiquities 20.17–96; Neusner 1965; Millar 1993.

entries.label: The garrison soldiers of Dura
entries.hint: The papyri of Dura show the Cohors XX Palmyrenorum, an auxiliary unit of Palmyrene archers of 1,000 men, with its pay rolls, duty rosters, the Feriale Duranum with the festival of the emperor, and the soldiers' private letters and requests for leave, the best evidence of an auxiliary regiment's daily life in the empire.
entries.note: Pap. Dura 100 (AD 219); Feriale Duranum; Nigel Pollard, Soldiers, Cities and Civilians in Roman Syria (2000).
